projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert D. Quinn was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oral history of World War II Veteran Robert D Quinn. Mr. Quinn served in the US Army with the 103rd Division, 410th Regiment, Company I. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was PFC. I am Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Quinn's home in West Lake, Ohio on October 13th, 2004. Robert was 79 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: I was living in Akron Ohio, I was living in, I was going to high school in 1941. I graduated from high school in June of 1942. And I enrolled in college at Akron University.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes. I listened to the radio. They put it on the radio almost immediately after it happened and then everybody else at that time got a map out and said where is Pearl Harbor? And we found it in the Hawaiian Islands. And the surprising thing is next month I am going to actually to Pearl Harbor to look at the Arizona and Missouri Battleships. I have never been there at all. I have never been west of San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really? So you have never been to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Right now I am going to a wedding, so it could be a happy occasion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I went there once several years ago. So you were still in high school, any of your classmates decide to drop out and join up?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: I was 17. Most of them were also 17. Many of them in the next year did volunteer or join. Many joined the Air Force or Army Air Corps and the Navy and I would imagine at the end of 1942, there were only two or three who were not in the service at that time because of health reasons.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your personal reaction when the war began for America? Did you think you would end up in it or did you think it would end before you got in it?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, I knew it was going to be a long war, but I did not, no one knows how long it would take. And we did not know the severity of the damage that had gotten to the Pacific fleets. We did not know how far the Japanese would be able to invade other countries. So we were not very well -- I thought it was going to last a long time. Therefore I knew, I was very -- hopefully it would end sometime, and of course, when it did end I was on my way to Japan, which was a place I didn't want to go, obviously.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember if the attack was a true surprise to you or did you have some idea that we were going to get into it?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, it was a true surprise. I have read all of the material, exactly what happened at Pearl Harbor, and also how the Japanese diplomats in Washington didn't let anyone know, even though they knew, that there was going to be an attack. I think America was caught off guard.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you graduated in June and went to school, started college in the fall of '42?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: In the fall of, in September at Akron U and then I had my last test on June 7th, a Saturday in 1942, and I entered the Army on the Monday, two days afterwards.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In '42 you went into the Army?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you --

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, no, no, 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '43. So you did get a year of college in?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: I got a year of college in, which probably helped me all the way through being in the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get involved, before you were drafted, get involved at all in the war effort?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember rationing being much of a problem?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Rationing, I don't believe started right in '42. I think it started somewhere just about the time I might have left for the service in '43. Because I was the person who would do all the buying for my family. And I don't remember having, dealing with rationing at all. So, from that time to the present time I do all the shopping, which I love to do. I am a shopper.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you got the word to report in June of '43?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes, and we reported to the recruiting center in Akron and left from there to go to Fort Hayes and then from Fort Hayes we arrived at a place in Texas called Camp Wolters, which is near a spa called Mineral Wells, Texas. And Mineral Wells is a small town, maybe two or three thousand people. It had however, it had Camp Wolters there and however the Mineral Wells was in a hotel and it was 12 floors high, which was to me, out in the middle of nowhere, a building that high, and it was to me quite incredible. Although, out in the middle of Texas, hot. And it was not the place to train, because it was just hot and hot and hot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of your first day of basic training?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Marching, marching, marching. The barracks were all surrounding a large quadrangle and we would march in every direction around this, sometimes just barely getting us together to prove we were marching, marching, marching. So, the first thing was a lot of marching.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned to an outfit at that point?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, at that particular point we were just a kind of replacement training company. And must have lasted thirteen weeks. And being a city boy, I had never had a rifle in my hands, up to the time I went to a rifle range. And I didn't have very good eyesight and being on the range, whenever you would miss something, they would wave a red flag. And after I would take a shot at a target, they would always claim that I didn't hit the target and wave the red flag. And I said, well, who cares? I didn't care whether I had a high score or a low score. But just because when I eventually got into the 103rd Division, they assigned me a Browning Automatic Rifle, called a BAR. And it fired many shots in one burst. And you didn't have to be very precise, which was good because I wasn't very precise. I was not a marksman, although I got a marksman badge, but that didn't mean anything. Everybody got one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any other stories or incidents from your training?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Probably, we had, they had in Texas they had these little insects called chiggers. And chiggers would go under your skin. And all you would see when they bit you is the end of their tail and then you had to some way dig them out. And most of the digging was done with some type of a knife. And you just get in there and dig them out. Of course, you had to bleed a little, but it was part of the self-protecting. So therefore, chiggers were just a tremendous problem. And that is the reason most people just didn't have any, except for around their hands or their neck, they kept their clothes right up. You had to protect yourself that way. We survived. And of course, then going into a town of Mineral Wells, there must have been 15,000 soldiers and the town was dry. And they had buses into town. There were free buses and you would just go in mainly to get a milk shake. Then there were not very many young women in the place for that number of men who were in the place. So it was just -- I have gone back to Mineral Wells and where Camp Wolters was is now an industrial park, which has all the roads in, because the roads were there. It had maybe only one or two buildings remaining of what was there in 1943. So it was a good training base. But at that time, I learned how to walk. But I had walked to school about two and a half miles every day, each way. So when I got hiking, hiking was a piece of cake, because I had walked a lot and therefore, it was easy to do for me. Many people found hiking a tremendous thing and passed out and to me it was just kind of a piece of cake.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you join the 103rd?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Well, it all had to do with what is called April Fool's Day. From Camp Wolters I had gone and you could go back to college in a group called the Army Special Training Program, ASTP, whose symbol was an old Greek light, like a torch. And therefore, we were sent from there, from Texas we were sent to Oklahoma University at Norman. And that also became a nice place to visit and we had classes. And we might have been there from two quarters, which must have been somewhere about September, '43 until April 1st, 1944. And they posted on April 1st a bulletin on all the walls, wherever you wanted to congregate around, what is going on, they had this notice, ASTP is being dropped and everybody in ASTP is going to be reassigned. And I said at the time, somebody really has a practical joke because this is April 1st. It's dated April 1st. This is a joke. It was not a joke. And so people left University of Oklahoma and many of them were assigned to the 103rd Division, which had Camp Howse, Texas. So that was, and they were in preparations to getting ready to go to final training to go to Europe. And then we had what is called a clash of cultures, because most of the non-coms in the 103rd Division had come from being in Louisiana with the 103rd Division and they were all regular Army and they were all Southern boys who were maybe not had graduated from high school and they had, were inundated with, in their platoon you might have 35 college students, whose attitude was this is ridiculous. And then we had a clash of cultures. Then many of us said do you have any questions? And of course, if you open it up like that to a group of college students they all had questions. And these questions were all pertinent questions, but which the non-coms could not answer because they were, they didn't quite see the irony of the questions. And so, it was it just kind of a challenging thing in regard to it. And so, all the way through, the friends I made in Company I were from two groups. Some of them were obviously those who had not been to college. But I would say 95 percent of the ones that I hung round with in the Army were ones who were in the, somewhere in the ASTP or in some other program that they were transferred to the infantry. So the irony of all of this was that we were always thinking of the practical way to do things, not the Army way, but the practical way of doing things. And of course, corporals and non -- and sergeants and especially first sergeants were always interested in doing it the "RA" way, the "Regular Army" way and that made it rather interesting. But it made life interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things were you studying at ASTP for that short time?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: We were studying just basically regular college subjects.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They hadn't picked a specialty for you yet?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, just a continuation of what I had at Akron U. Norman is, the pastor of the church I went to in Akron, Ohio, his sister lived in Oklahoma City, Okie City, and Oklahoma City at that time, it still is, there is so many oil derricks all over the city that where it would be considered in this area an eye sore. For there it wasn't an eye sore, it was a money-maker. And therefore, people with oil wells were guaranteed a lot of money and therefore, so I visited the sister of the pastor and eventually my mother came down to visit in Norman from Akron and she was kind of being chaperoned by the pastor's sister who was ____________ the people that had and oil well in your backyard was a little richer than an ordinary person. I enjoyed my time at Norman. And many of the -- I have pictures of always about every class who were involved with ASTP at Norman. Where there might be in one picture maybe 160 people, all identified, but not myself. I'm not in any of the pictures.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you taking the pictures?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, these are --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just the regular photographs?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Just 12 inches by 36.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, okay, camera type or whatever.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And there were about six high and it must have been on the stand, that type of thing and taking it. And they were all identified and the city where they were and also the University they had come from were identified. But I got those pictures, but I haven't really been any success in identifying anybody.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: If we find one unidentified person, it might be you.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, I must have been absent the day that they took the pictures. But that is life, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now Camp Howse was near Gainsville, Texas?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me about the life of the camp or in Gainsville when you got a chance to go into town?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Well, I have been back to Gainsville so I know how it is now. They have a museum in Gainsville, pretty much like a 103rd, and there is two other divisions who were training at Howse at the same time. 83rd and maybe a third division, and they are putting in, trying to put up a monument for all three Divisions in that particular Gainsville area. I just thought of it as another typical Texan town. And it had, obviously, Camp Howse extended all the way toward the Red River in Oklahoma, the border with Oklahoma. So was it was a large area and it had a lot of artillery training there and a lot of hiking and a lot of -- So they were really getting people ready for extended tour of walking and such. That is how it was. Everybody knew that they were going overseas and therefore, they were kind of, you paid a little attention, more attention to your non-coms at the time, but not that much more. You were just coexisting was really it. And then of course, they, the non-coms, they after a while said what can you do with these guys? They have attitude. Here is what whole group of people and they never said it, but, they had choice words for people that went to school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you were not too far from Denton or Dallas and I have heard stories of the guys that would go in --

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yeah, there is Big D and Little D. Little D was Denton. And Denton was the home of a teacher's college at Denton. And they had at camp Howse they had USOs. And they would bring in the student girls from Denton and they would actually bring them in to what were converted cattle cars. And which where on the flat part, it wasn't a bus, it was a cattle car, and they would bring them in like maybe 100 at a time to the USO dances. So many people would go to the dances. I was not a dancer, so I didn't, I was not a person who had much contact with girls, except after that maybe thirty seconds I'd say would you like to sit and talk? I was a talker, not a dancer. And so I never knew anyone really specific there except that they all were very pleasant. And many people went to the USO dances because they could, it was a place where you could get free writing material where you could write home and all that. And I tried to do that as often as possible. But I wasn't much of a dancer, but I did go to the dance just looking. I was a looker. But not a dancer. Then of course, we also had movies, a lot of movies taking place. And they were, in present day standards were movies, they were almost like cut-and-dried. This is what you have to do and it's almost like teaching you something you either already knew or you're not supposed to talk about, where you are going, and keep quiet an all of that and that is obviously how you should do it. But then you'd have maybe a thousand people in these large theaters which were just the whole series of wooden benches from front to back, maybe two aisles, one on the right and one on the left. And then the projector was a little higher. And the screen must have been 20 by 50 feet and the training films during the day and they did some have movies at night. And I went to the movies then and I have been a life-long goer to movies. And my wife doesn't go to any movies, so I go to movies on Tuesday, because they are cheaper. And then the training, and then when it got down to the very end they had what is called training for amphibious training and so, we were bringing up into Oklahoma. And then, had these flat barges that had 20 people on each side of them. And you were, and they were kind of up-side-down at one particular point and they would say, okay, everybody at the count of three, everybody lift. And this was a maybe a four, five or six ton, but with so many people lifting you could actually lift it up. However, one of my fingers, it's bent over because somebody dropped the thing and I didn't get my finger out in time. So the end of my finger has always been bent over just a little because of, it must have been some form of a barge type of thing. So I didn't get my finger out. And of course, I did it on the wrong hand. I am right-handed, so left hand didn't get me out, except if you have a big bandage on your one hand, you still can't carry your rifle, so it got me out of carrying the rifle for a while. Gold brick I wasn't, but I wasn't totally enthusiastic. So going overseas that, first of all we went from Howse all the way up to Camp Upton -- not Upton, but Camp Shanks on the Hudson. And from there they were going to load us on ships. But we had about, I had one pass to New York City. And so I went with a group of friends and I went to a play. And I have seen the movie of the play on many, many times on one of channels and it was a story about someone, it was a story about someone coming to Ireland, an Irish story, I being Irish, so it dealt with -- The name is one I don't remember right now, but it's the story of kind of a town that is forgot. It was a kind of a tail about Ireland. It was, to me it was a very popular one at the time and I enjoyed seeing Broadway at that time. But I was not a drinker. And I think that helped me in many ways that I did not drink. Many soldiers were, you'd go with them and you'd have to help them back on the bus, help them back to camp, help them back. So there were a lot of people who overdid their drinking, but that was part of being young, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you shipped out in, if I remember correctly, early October 6th I believe of '44?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Something like that and we were on the General J R Brook.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: In fact I have a picture of the ship in one of these books here and found out a little bit about this. And it was, surprisingly enough, when the first time I have ever been in a large boat on an ocean and what is kind of surprising is that we would see certain things, we would see sailboats. And these were sailboats that almost like they had been from the time of Columbus. Portuguese fisherman were sailing their boats, sailboats, but they were ocean-going. But it was toward Newfoundland and the fishing was better at that particular time. Because they were so small no one would even waste a torpedo on them at this particular time. And then in the middle of the ocean you would see, off to the distance you would see smoke, black smoke on the horizon, which was a way of bringing the war to you, that here was a ship that had gone down that was burning. And therefore, somebody, another ship had been sunk by, submarine had taken it. And then if a storm came up, and all, we had oh, some destroyer escorts, but not very many. We might have had in our convoy maybe 10, 12 different ships and the storm had gotten rough and, you know, all you had to do was look out and sometimes you wondered how our ship missed the other ships, because we were passing in the storm back and forth. And I thought to myself someone is looking after us, because the ship, it's almost like you would collide in the storm. It was that close. And I thought to myself, somebody is looking after us. We went around Gibraltar and got to North Africa. And North Africa looks like a desert, because there didn't seem to be any, it was very orange, sandy. But then our ship went, hugged the coast of North Africa and then headed north toward what eventually was Marseille and we knew that was where we were headed. But the most severe storm we had was in the Mediterranean. It's like the severe storms, a lot of severe storms in Lake Erie because it's shallow, more severe than they are in the middle of the ocean. And that is very true. We had a very severe storm in the Mediterranean. And we ended and came up and I saw this large church on the French coast. And I thought to myself, where would that be. And because of activity around that it had been that it was the largest church in Toulon, which is east of Marseille, and which is a French Naval base that had been recaptured. And then from there we were surprised, we headed west to Marseille. And then in Marseille was the port of -- a lot of devastation there. Lot of piers were down, lot of bridges were down. And we had to disembark by way of rope ladders and with heavy field packs. And that was not easy, but it's like everything else, you get through that. And when you get on level ground then they said okay, we're going to march you up into the hills. They didn't tell us it was twenty miles away. But we went on to a barren peninsula overlooking Marseille. It had nothing in it. It was like rocks. And they said okay, we're going to pitch your tent here. You couldn't put a stick in that ground more than two inches before you hit rock. It was almost, it was whoever picked this out would even they said, it's typical Army. Nobody here was finding out how easy it was. But everybody lined up in there and they pitched their tent there and we got through it and so. And they gave us what is called "port duty", unloading ships. And how they would do that, they would unload with, over the side of the ship they would unload big cartons. And then they'd drop them down to the dock. And they didn't have anybody to move them around except by manpower. So there you were, they would break open these particular cans and they are all number ten cans. And they would line up 25 people or 40 people or 100 people in a long line from the side the ship to a place they could get a truck. And they would have to pass these number ten cans just like a fireman's brigade. And then there was always somebody said okay, I've had enough of this, I am going to find what is in these cans. So we had people who then dropped the cans. And of course, as soon as you dropped the can, it couldn't be used again. So they would say okay five minute or ten minute break. And you'd get your bayonet and you opened up the can with about ten different stabs and then you'd pry the number ten can back. Crushed pineapple. It was crushed pineapple on one of the sides, it was oozing out. And of course it is somewhat of a laxative. So therefore it was forbidden fruit, because we're not supposed to did it, but somebody did it. And so, everybody had some kind of spoon. And so anyhow, we were stealing, but it was, at that time it wasn't considered stealing, it just was an accident happened. Then we got serious. And they loaded us on trucks and they took us up the valley, the river valley. And the roads were -- My geography came back to me that I had studied. And one of the towns in Southern France at one time was the head of the church. The Catholic Church had moved from Rome to Avignon in Southern France. And here I was looking at the, other than the back of the six by six truck, looking out where, and of course, at the beginning or the end of every town, they had their name on a sign. And I saw this sign Avignon and I said here was history. We're passing it by and I am not even having a chance to stop here. Because I knew the history of Avignon. And of course then we went, from there we went north and finally came to a place called Dijon. And we camped in the city park, the city center park. This became a bivouac area. And then from that bivouac area we got in the trucks the next morning and we were going toward the front. And so we kept going through some small towns and eventually we got into the forest and Vosges Mountains. And as we were going by, because we were always looking out the back of the truck, you said you always knew where you were going past, we kept saying what are all these trees, what of these trees by the side of the road? Well, they weren't at the side of the road, they had been blocking the road and someone had moved them off to the side of the road. This was how the Germans stopped the original trucks going through. It was just cut down a tree. Very easy to do. They had some kind of, or even with a saw you could cut the tree down and plop it right in. And so we saw that and then you get to a place and off the trucks. It was about 6:00 o'clock or 7:00 o'clock in the evening and it was getting dark. And then we started walking in single file. And eventually that particular day and night we relieved an American division, the 5th Division in the Vosges Mountains. And then the war started for us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that first night on the line?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Oh, yes. Well, we couldn't see very much but when you opened the next day we were in kind of like a little shed, not shed, someone had already cut a few trees down and put some trees and boughs on the top of it, so we ended up in kind of a protected place. And the first thing getting up in the morning and looking around, because we don't know where we were, came upon a dead body, a German. And that was, of course, the war, the shock. The surprising thing is that many Americans this had happened, collected watches off dead soldiers. Whether they collected rings or they could see the stuff. There were some people that just were collectors and that was kind of foreign to me that a person should -- a person is dead, that way you can't do anything about it, and but, then we were in the forest and, of course, the Germans had their artillery were doing what are called "shell bursts." And they had killed many, the first in our platoon, in our company were killed were shell bursts and came from above. And so, in this particular stuff --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did shell bursts actually explode at a higher altitude or is that the trees?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, they hit the trees on the way down, and therefore, at that time, they hit a tree, it would splinter and they went everywhere. And so therefore, that is how many shrapnel deaths were caused. And this one particularly was a close friend was Francis Postapack, Frank Postapack and he was a close friend.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember, was he killed by a shell burst?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yeah, he was. And he must have been killed within five, three or four or five days of getting on line. So he was the first member of our company to die. And you only heard about that, later they said "Frank got it." So, after the war, another friend of ours, he was a person who went to a went to school in Rensselaer, New York. And it's called Rensselaer Poly Institute. So he was, you just had to know certain ones because they would maybe be the ones that would go to church with you on Sunday and things like that. And then after the war, his mother was most bitter in regard to the war, that gave her son for -- most of the mothers even, today, their reaction to the war, sometimes they said well, it's for the country, but other people are kind of bitter about it. And a mutual friend of ours who visited her after the war, she was most bitter. Although he talked to Frank's sister and the sister and her husband came and visited Frank's burial place in France and that kind of helped, I think, the family making some kind of -- but he recommended this, if he could to go, because that kind of, he was buried under a beautiful spot in Alsace. So, we got through the war and for the first, I would say 70 days, we were under, we had artillery fire over our heads. And which meant you were somewhere close to the front. It was lot of war and then we never went through cities, we were always in the hills and then avoiding everybody. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the first day you were under close enemy fire, not from artillery, but from a fire fight or something?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes. It happened when we just came out of the hills. We were kind of in the spot where it was, you might describe it as a plain area. And we were on a raid and there was an exchange of fire between the Germans and us. And people were hit and then we'd pick them up and carried them back. But they were probably a hundred yards from where you were. When the battalion officer said okay, we're going back, you go back very quickly. Yeah, but it was under fire that way. But surprisingly, so many of the deaths occurred just in the middle of fields, mines. And that was just because you couldn't see them, and you step on a trip wire and it was -- at the convention we were mentioning that the way we got through, most of us, we really put it down as luck. There was somebody else, it wasn't us. And I think that that is how I attributed it. It wasn't because we were better soldiers than them. It was just they were unlucky and we were quite lucky, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particularly close calls for you, personally?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: I never got a purple heart, because when they had these shell bursts and the shell bursts, we had all of shrapnel coming down in the trees, and one of them fell on my wrist, a piece of inch-square shrapnel and I flicked it off like that. It broke the skin. And the person, I said, well, didn't do any damage, didn't make blood. Technically I would have gotten a purple heart, but I didn't apply for it. And I thought to myself, that was nothing. But later on, if a person had accumulated points, you could accumulate five points for having a purple heart. And a purple heart didn't have to be the thing, questioning certain people's purple heart that they had, and such as that, many people had shrapnel and it was hot, and it was on your hand, and I just flicked it off. It could be that I just had tough skin at the time, but it didn't break, and right now, I can just touch myself and I get a mark on my skin. It was just a matter of luck. So when that would happen, you know, the shrapnel would hit your head, your helmet, and thank God, but never really was seriously injured. But I did see people, many people dead.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the 410th involved in the campaign for Seligenstadt?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Seligenstadt, we were in the area of Seligenstadt and let me give you this particular part.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Most of this early fighting for those listing was the Alsace Lorraine region, correct?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes, they were in Alsace. I would say most of ours, except for one was in Alsace. Here is a map of the area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So I don't know how news would have traveled between regiments, but did you hear anything about what had happened at Seligenstadt?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: We did know that at Seligenstadt there were prisoners taken.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And we didn't hear how many there were. Let me see if I can find it. This was the path.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Here is Seligenstadt.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes, that is Seligenstadt. This is a region of Hobart was in the mountains and that is where our company was attacked when the Germans were on the top of a hill. And then we went from there to Dambach, which is right at the edge of the plain. And then from there we went to Shirrahler (ph) and then I think what happened is we came up too close to Seligenstadt and at that particular time, that is when the people were captured at that time in that particular area. But I have visited Seligenstadt since that time. I have some pictures of it and churches and all of that. But then we have all the ones that were killed and where they were killed and so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you in that Vosges Mountain area until what early December, probably?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Early December, and then they moved us from there up to, up to the northern part of Alsace, just on the way to Germany. And so, we were moving probably in late, oh, I would say that it was somewhere around, you have heard others maybe talk about Klembach. That was in late December, 19th of December. So, then we, from that particular area we moved up to into, across the border. Then one of our soldiers on our list, who was killed either by a German sniper or by an America sniper. Who knows? And he was the last one who was killed in our particular company. But then we were told, we're taking you out of here because they are shortening the lines, because that he was the Battle of the Bulge. So they shortened our lines, and so they said we're going to retreat to the Möhne River and then it must have been about 25 miles, and we were going to retreat over really a day or day and a half. So people were on just walking in reverse and headed backwards and we left. The French people were most upset because the Germans were coming back. And it is, and I talked, in one of my trips back, I talked to a family who had been liberated in December, and then had been, Germans had come back and then they had been reliberated in March 15th. And they were not very kindly toward Americans. You were here and you left. They didn't quite understand the big picture. And of course, who would? But they were the very ones who were not, they were in the area near Muerzbahler (ph) was the family that I particularly was involved, right in here. This is the Möhne River line in Muerzbahler was is the hometown of someone who I knew in high school and his family came from Muerzbahler in the early 1900s, but they had relatives back there. And so, they were in Muerzbahler, they had been liberated, and then the Germans came back and the Germans who came back were most brutal. Because, well, they were liberated, they actually were, theoretically they were going to recapture Strasbourg in part of the process, but they never did. But there was no love loss between the Germans and the French. And especially when the French were so happy to have been liberated and then they were back under the German Army. It was a very difficult time for them. And I think many tried to leave at the same time we did. Didn't quite make it, so there was a lot of animosity I am sure at that time and there was after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Although the group that we have gone back and are the sponsors for a lot of the, they are called the Liberation Society, are actually living in the Pfaffenhofen area. And that was one of the places that I have been back to with the family that I stayed in their home in a place called Muerzbahler, the Kern (ph) family. And they are good friends and such and so. But the people were liberated twice. They didn't quite understand why, because they suffered a lot in that period of three months. And it wasn't a good feeling at the time. But I am sure that everything in a period of time from 1945 to 1990, when I went back there, the family, everything was, had been changed quite a bit. Alsace is a very modern part of France. They are, they are into just about everything modern you can have. They have supermarkets over there that were bigger than anything we had in this country at the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you often basically hold the line then for about three months?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yeah, hold the line, with a lot of being out on guard duty out in the hills and sometimes they would send patrols out to see where the Germans were. And just really just to find out where they were and how many there were. And it was fairly quiet. And there were a lot of refugees in the towns that we were in. And so there were a lot of families that were kind of doubled up. And we also, was many times we took over their house or their downstairs or such. And so many of them were living in the basements and we were in their comfortable beds if we slept in a bed at night. Otherwise, we were in a foxhole. And when they chose these foxholes, these foxholes were way out in the middle of nowhere and you were quite exposed at that particular time. Like they were underground, but you kind of sat in it, where you basically were kneeling in them. You were kind of a sitting duck for anybody. But you could see. Because that was the first time we ever had what they called search lights. They would have search lights and they would have low hanging clouds. And with these search lights, actually banked on the low hanging clouds, it was almost like day. Therefore, in the middle of the night you could see half a mile. You could see anybody approaching. So therefore, I always thanked God for these search lights. I see these search lights that are like opening a new car dealer or any kind of a search light for an opening of anything, I said thank God they are using them for this purpose, because they were using them in France just to illuminate the skies. And that is something I had not thought about but it turned out to be a very fortunate thing, the search lights. And it only happened like when the clouds were at like 2000 feet. Low clouds, you could almost have it searching, go up and down and up and down. It was amazing to me, but somebody had that. And of course they were about a mile and a half behind the lines. And I think maybe some of the Germans tried to take them out, but they were on most of the time. Especially around Christmas time because it was like, Christmas was -- And we were so close to the German lines at Christmastime we could hear caroling at the church, at the churches. Now these were not German churches, they were French churches. But apparently, they had services in them so the Germans let them have their church services, because many of the German soldiers were probably at the church service, as well. But you could hear some of the choirs just faintly, if you paid attention. So, it was rather interesting that even at that time, it's just God's on both sides of this line. And wondering in regard to it, it was irony, a lot of ironies like that. And of course, also, the French at Christmastime would have a tree and these, inside the house, and there had been a tree maybe they had cut down and they stood it up there. But they actually lit real candles. They didn't have lights. They had real candles. And I thought to myself, one of those trees falling over would burn the whole house down. But of course, they all said they would light them, like we're going to light the candles. And they lit all the candles maybe for four or five minutes, sung a hymn or choral and then they would go with their little thing and put them all out. But it was in the house I was staying that we had a Christmas tree with lights on, and even though we were right outside the town, where the foxholes were that we were in, and at any time we couldn't have stopped with our rifles the Germans if they had tanks. But basically it was a quiet zone until about the 15th of March when everyone was going to be the final battle. And that is, again, we lost some soldiers on that particular day. March 15th and 16th, when the big shift came.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the invasion into Germany crossing the Rhine?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No, no, no, that was retaking all of this land.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Retaking that land.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes, all the land had been taken and I have a battle map from the French Army at the time and they showed all of the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was retaking the land still in France, right?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes, still in France, up to the, up to the, up towards not the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Same difference.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: -- here all together. And then this is a, copy of the, this is what the plaque is, that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: -- how I decided in 1990 -- 1994, 50th anniversary of D-Day, that we should have, possibly honor those who died. And the best way to honor them was to have plaques in France. This was Ervillers. And this was in Hobart and this is, this is in a German Lutheran Church, but this is right next to the World War I plaque of France, World War II plaque of France. This was the Americans. And of course, I had to make certain that it was in correct French. And I thought it had to be in French, because what good would it be putting everything in English?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: So there was a marble company in Akron and this marble company I went down there because they were ones that I had walked by their plant for years when I was in high school and I had gone down to the plant in Cleveland, the monument places. And I had an idea of what I wanted done and they quoted me a price and I said that is beyond me. So I went through this Daley Monument. And it used to be in downtown Akron, but now it's out on the Northeast side near I76. And I went to this company and I said I need, I'd like to have a couple plaques made and they are to honor fellow company people who died in the war and they are going to be very much alike. Their names will be different, because one is going to be in a church in the mountains, the Vosges Mountains at Hobart and the other one is going to be Ervillers which was where this March 15th battle took place. And where I have been back to Ervillers and I have been back to Hobart, I have not been back to Hobart, I have been back to, very close to Ervillers. But anyhow I said I wanted the Cactus patch, and tri-color and the America flag and a cross of David and a star -- the cross, and it had to be in French. They said well, we're not very good here at French. Whatever you want it to be, you find out how it correctly should be, and how you would put it in memory of. And I went to the Magnificat High School, which is down the street, and I went to the French teacher and I said how will I say this and where should the accent marks be? And of course, then the liberation of Hobart on this particular date that was the battle of Hobart, first three were actually killed in this particular battle, and the other nine were in the liberation of Alsace. And so and then, of course, the names all had to be there. And then they list their, they put the company and the regiment and the division this way in French. It's not the 103rd Division, it's Division 103 and 410th Infantry. And the fellow said well, and we have some black, too, black marble. I said I want it to be, it's as big as four of these together. So rather than them being eight and a half by 11, it's 11 by 17 and that is how we decided on the size. And then I said they did it all by computer. Everything is cut and they make the, obviously, they do this by just simply marking it and drawing it in with a computer. And then they cut it with diamond drills. And it kind of looks that particular way. Then of course, how to get it over to France. And I went to, called various airlines and I said I have this package I want delivered to probably Strasbourg, France, so everybody would get it to Paris, because they would take it overland from Paris to Strasbourg. I said no, I want it delivered to Strasbourg by air. And they said we don't go that way, and I said well, I'll try someplace else. So I tried about five or six airlines. And then I went to one person and they said I have an idea. And he said we have some, I have a friend who is in this delivery business in France and they might just be very happy to deliver it personally to the church yard. They'd fly it into Frankfurt and then they'd fly it from Frankfurt to Strasbourg Airport and then they would, they have their own delivery service in Alsace. And I said well, that is fine. Yes. I said, what would this cost? He said, what is this for? I said this is to honor Americans for the liberation of France. He said this will be a public service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And so from the airport in Strasbourg it was delivered by truck to the church in Hobart and the church in Ervillers and then they were going to then have it put wherever they, wherever the church wanted it to be or whatever. And of course, the airline was Lufthansa.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: That is kind of an irony.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: A German national carrier for the good will of the French people were willing to take an America donation. Of course, the one thing you never want to do, because the first thing was let's call the French Embassy in Washington. And they said, transferred my call and said this is, we're transferring you to the general in charge of monuments. I said, no. We don't want to -- he said oh, this all has to go through the State Department. And I said, no, no, no. We don't want to do it this particular way, because that is what had happened in the monument in Pfaffenhofen and the monument in Strasbourg. Everything had to go through the State Department and then to the French government and all of that, and the bureaucracy, just simply. So we got them there. Surprisingly enough, I had also, you might have met him, he was at the 103rd reunion, Arnie Marcero (ph). He was one of the two who went to the dedication in France, one of them, to this particular dedication in France, and was well received. And now, when people go back to Alsace, they not only go back to see the 103rd monument in Saffier (ph), they go to see the 103rd Division monument in Pfaffenhofen. They always take a little side trip and say we're just going to drive up here to show you a little monument here in Ervillers and that is the one that we put there. And it was just so -- And the pastor of this church, first name is Patrick, which is an Irish name.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Saint Patrick. And I thought to myself, oh, the way we sometimes work these things and it comes out. And I have had several letters from him and in the process of getting it all done. And then had also had this contact in Ervillers, the family I stayed with. And so I had a phone call. I would call the Kern family in Ervillers and they would deal with their own pastor, Patrick Herren. So it was like having a personal person doing it for you. And of course, how they packaged all of this was this packaging company out near Cleveland Air -- Hopkins Airport and I said how you are you going to take this and make certain that it doesn't break? Well, they said, we're going to build a case around it and they packaged it in wood.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And so they really put in the marble, they had wood on both sides of it and they have it all screwed together at the top and the only thing you could possibly break it is if they dropped the whole wooden container.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: So anyhow, that particular person did it so well, and he was the person who arranged the idea of getting it sent by Lufthansa, and thought to myself, well, that is an interesting way how the world happened. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else do you remember about that March 15th battle?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Oh, it was a battle of -- we never had more artillery support. They started maybe at 5:00 in the morning and kept going for three hours steady and then we were told to take off and we came to Ervillers. And that is where we ran into our first resistance and that is where two or three of the soldiers were killed in Ervillers. And then from then on we said it was push, push, push, push and gradually the resistance became less and less. So when we got to the German border there was practically no resistance whatsoever. Because the Division had sent some armored task forces ahead who really had disrupted the whole German Army in the back and they were, in at that particular time they were, started to, most of the units were simply surrendering.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: So, at that -- and from then we went into, we were, we had a watch on the Rhine. We were on the Rhine River. And we had kind of foxholes right on the edge of the Rhine. And we were just to make certain that the Germans didn't come back over the Rhine. And I am sure the Germans, we don't really think they were going to try this because that would take boats and all of that and they didn't have anything like that. So it was kind of a not very certain that -- it wasn't much really battle in regards to it. The last place that the Division was in a battle was in the probably the outskirts of the Alla (ph) Alps. In the region near the, getting down toward Innsbruck. There were a few last battles and after that the war was over. And the interesting thing was with a BAR they said okay, the BAR would go first and down this curvy mountain road. And everybody is to walk on the side of the road and here, Bob -- Quinn, you go out there and lead us right down the middle of the road and you have your BAR and you shoot the BAR if you see any problems. And I said okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And so by that time we were going down to a very famous village, which I knew already about. They said what is the next town over? They said well, it's Oberammergau. Oh, I know the town. It's the passion play town. Sometimes you know too much. And of course, we had heard stories. There were not any passion plays in 1940, but there had been in 1930. And so it turned out that the most beautiful sight, their houses in Oberammergau have murals all over the houses, religious murals. And they all had balconies. And the most beautiful sight was white sheets hanging from every balcony.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: So again, you lucked out and such.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And so then we came from there and we got farther east and stopped. And the last time I think anyone fired their rifles were somewhere in the, just outside in the air field in the Inn Valley. And that was the end. And so we were very pleased that the war was over. And we also took duty in the small town of Notters (ph) which is next to a little town called Muters (ph). I have been back to both of these towns. And the German read-out had been in the mountains of Austria. And so, we had, we were kind of garrisoning the town and then they called you up to this particular center of town and then there were the German soldiers coming down, officers still had their arms and they were all surrendering. Now, so there were many colonels and generals and they were coming down. And even at that particular point almost didn't say -- they said "We're officers, we get special treatment". And but, they -- Soon they all just passed on, just passed them down, and somebody at the end of the line took care of them. But that was the end of the war. And it was everybody, most everybody was very happy And we went in occupation in what is called the San Leonard Valley (sic). And the San Leonard Valley, now it would be a ski resort, but they had, at that point they had, it was like they had schools, special concentration for German girls who were either prostitutes or they were just simply -- and they had a kind of school. And therefore, it was, you don't know whether or not they were, how they got into the situation that they were in, but they had special names for these particular places. And you felt sorry for anybody who got involved with it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have much contact with the German people either before or after the war actually ended?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: We stayed in Luters (ph) in an inn.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And I got to know the daughter, got to know the innkeeper and his innkeeper daughter and she was maybe 16 at the time. And she would be -- and we had to walk, there was a swimming hole maybe a mile, two kilometers away. And somebody got a Jeep and they would take everybody over to the swimming hole and they always would take her along. And all I can remember at the time is that she must have had the only wool bikini in Austria. And she obviously liked to wear this, because it brought attention to her. But the only thing is that because it was made out of wool, that the moths had gotten to it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: So, it was not all there. And therefore, no one would tell her that. Like she didn't know already. But anyhow it was rather revealing. And but she was, since that particular time when we went back to Austria in 1991 with my wife, we stayed in the same inn. And the inn is now a three star or four star hotel. And that was this was the only, well, it was so modern that the front door would open if you got near it, one of those automatic door openers. And I had corresponded with her with Christmas cards and things afterward and her father had passed away and had went into business. He was buried in the church yard, which was right next to the inn. And she took us to where he was buried. And it was kind of touching that she was -- They were in a part of Austria that were under French occupation and it was rougher than America occupation, because the French didn't put up with anything, because they had been --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: But when we went back and they had three, the meeting was in three languages. It was in English, German, and what other language?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: French?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: English, German -- and I don't know.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Innsbruck in the route to where going south?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: To Italy.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Yes. So it is Italy, Italian newspapers, first English newspaper we read, and then also German newspapers. So therefore, their menu was in three languages and they were catering basically to businessmen. And we were treated very well, and because someone who had corresponded with her and she must have taken a liking to us. And it was just to see her again. And so at that time she would have been maybe, must have been in upper 60s, but she had taken over and her daughter, she had, her kids were taking care of the inn. But she was a real big businessman and doing quite well in that particular town. So it was good to see that this little place that we had stayed in became really like a tourist thing in the mountains. And they still had, at that time in '90 they still had the trollies. And the trollies would go downtown Innsbruck, up the mountain, when they go up the mountain their path is always zigzag, zigzag, so the rise, to make it rise. And they had a regular schedule and you would get on there and you would ride to the middle of downtown Innsbruck, where I am always looking for castles and such. And that is, surprisingly enough, where they had one of the emperors had their had their summer palace in downtown Innsbruck and they had a ballroom on the second floor. And this ballroom is so large, they had a picture of their 12 kids. And each picture was about eight foot by 12 feet wide this one giant pennant. And of course, then you look at Maria, Marie Antoinette, the French woman.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And then others were there. And Maria Teresa, that is -- and then, they had inside, right next to the church there is a Saint James Cathedral and inside the Saint James Cathedral is this giant sarcophagus. And I said well, who was this? It was, it says "Reichsmarschall." Now, who do you know who was called Reichsmarschall? Goering.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Goering, okay.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: But this was a Reichsmarschall of the German Navy in World War I.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: He was not a Nazi. But he was buried there and it says Reichsmarschall, which was his title. And his, he had been the head of the German Navy in the First World War. And the during the Second World War, his name had appeared on a battleship, which was not the Bismark, but a battleship that was run aground in Buenos Aires early in World War II.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And therefore, I put everything together and interesting way of how people remember history. History is frequently done by the leaders.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. So you said you were in the occupation forces for a while and then you were possibly headed for Japan?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Then we were told that we were going to be transferred to Japan, so they brought us back through Le Havre, giving us the opportunity to go to the see the cathedral, which is not the cathedral at Le Havre, but the cathedral at Rouen, it was one of the larger cathedrals and we went to that cathedral. And then I got the chance to go to Paris for the first time. And I enjoyed that very much. And then we went back and then we went on shipboard. And by the time we got to Boston Harbor the war was over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing that news?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Of course we had heard the news prior to that, that the atomic bomb had been dropped in two places. And even at that point there was an argument as to whether they should have dropped the bomb. My view has always been that it would have saved a million lives at least and therefore, there wasn't really a question in regard to it. Although when they put the exhibit on at the Smithsonian in Washington, in the last ten years there had been quite a bit of the discussion as to whether it was really needed. But that is always looking at things from the back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: I had to go to get discharged and they sent me all the way to camp Atterbury. And they, I had two bags with me. I had a little duffle bag and a big giant one that everybody carried. It must have been about three and a half foot high, had a couple bags on it. And it had everything that I had wanted to save during the war and they were taking a train from there to Cleveland. And I must have gone in to check on the schedule or something, and when I came back out, my big duffle bag had been stolen by another American GI, and I thought to myself, well, that is life. My uniform, everything I wore. So therefore, when I came home I did not really have only a partial uniform I was wearing. And so, but the bag that I kept, the smaller bag, had inside of it a giant Nazi flag which I had picked up in, I think it was in Oberammergau. It was about four foot, five feet by eight feet. And the question is what can you do with a Nazi flag? You can't display it, because people would say what is with this?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: So I have been looking around, I wanted to, how to get rid of something. And surprisingly, it was good material and it didn't, in a total of forty years, it didn't, fifty years, forty years, it didn't disintegrate at all. Every time I would take it out, it was just as good condition as it was before. So, when we were going to get a -- our company had, one of the persons was named Gene Wise.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Gene Wise had died under the following circumstances: Some way in a rough basement, he -- Everybody carried two hand grenades on their lapels. And one of these hand grenades, in falling in front of him, with about twenty people in the room, it fell off his lapel. And he fell upon it to save everybody's life. It was decided by the officers of our company that we had had too many self-inflicted wounds, finger, toes, which is a very common thing to happen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: So at the time they said, everybody said Gene should have gotten a medal. And the company commander then said he would not put in for a medal, even though he was reminded about it many, many times, because it would set a bad precedent. So, through the help of others, I helped to, I am the letter writer, and so we assembled all the evidence about Gene Wise. And then that was the added to our book that he got the Soldier's Medal at _____________, Missouri and that several of the soldiers whose lives they saved were able to be there. And they gave the Soldier's Medal, a Colonel from Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: Kansas is right next to Missouri, just across the Missouri river, he came down and he awarded it to the next of kin of Gene Wise because we -- and how do you think we got a medal 45 years later?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Hum...

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: You call your representatives.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, right.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And one of our friends of Company I, used to come to all the reunions, he had a very close friend of his and he was the Representative from Iowa. And his name is Jim Leach, very prominent Republican. And through Jim Leach and through another person who lives in the Saint Joe's area, another Congresswoman, they were able to go, by-pass all the regulations and get this awarded. And it tells in here, I'll give you a copy of this, about all the testimony --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: -- of where, First Sergeant's letter, he was still alive, he is still alive now, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: -- it was all based upon the sergeants wanted to give him an award, but they, the Company Commander would not. And this is what the Soldier's Medal looked like. So we were able to get it through and then I traveled to Kansas city and went to the dedication ceremony myself --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: -- along with a couple other, there might have been five of us from Company I who were there. And not his parents, but his aunts were there and cousins, and so they were all very happy that we were able to complete that transaction. It's like fighting City Hall.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Well, very good. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: That is about it, except I am enjoying retirement very much. And I like to write and I like to put together books and you can, the company, the book about World War I might interest you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And this is about Gene Wise, which was, which had just happened in, I think it was -- What is the date on it?

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: That was exactly --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That is 55 years later. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: 55 years later. So sometimes you get things corrected. You see now that some people who were awarded, many blacks were awarded -- denied medals are now getting them. Because it was, oh, just the Army was all white at that time. The Company I was all, all the Divisions were. But to show you how little it changed among people, I went back to Pfaffenhofen in 1991 for the dedication of the ceremony, and stayed with the French family, the Kern family in Ervillers, and they used to have celebrations. Now, there was attached to the 103rd Division for a long period of time was a Tank Destroyer Battalion, 761. I think it got a Presidential citation for the whole unit. Then, when we went back there for the dedication, a member who had been in the 761, a black man from a place in New York City, brought his grandson and his son with him just to show him them where he was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: And he was at the banquet and the attitude of many in the 1945 or '44 toward blacks has not changed very much in 50 years. And I thought there is just some people who will never learn. And I, I overheard comments about him that they, you know -- And I thought to myself, boy, can't people forget? He was a soldier, the same as you and I. In fact, his Tank Destroyer Battalion saved the whole 411th Regiment at Zutzendorf. And you are still worried about this person being equal to you? You have a worry in regard to people who are -- and I just, the term "ornery American", this is a term that is one which, there is some people act that way and never have learned. And you feel so sorry about people that like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert D. Quinn
sp.p: But that is, and they were all members of the 103rd Division. And their view of life and their view of the world and the view of the war is one which is, showed very little progress in regard to -- It's almost as if I am better than you. God made me better than you. I'll always be better than you. Everybody is in God's image. Some people are not quite. So, having a good philosophy and being able to understand this, hopefully I have imparted many of the ideas I have to my kids, of which I have seven. [Interview Concluded]
